overview: Muslim rule in Sicily grew from a conquest begun in 827 and changed between Aghlabid, Fatimid and locally rooted Kalbid governments. Palermo became a major center. The map’s 900 to 1100 label spans several political phases; the island was neither conquered in one day nor governed by one uninterrupted dynasty.

periods.title: Conquest and provincial government
periods.summary: North African armies gradually displaced Byzantine rule; authority later passed from the Aghlabids to the Fatimids.

periods.title: Kalbid government
periods.summary: From the mid-tenth century, hereditary Kalbid governors ruled from Palermo under Fatimid supremacy.

periods.title: Fragmentation and Norman conquest
periods.summary: Local rivalries weakened centralized rule. The Normans took Palermo in 1072 and completed their conquest in 1091.

items.text: Researchers analyzed 134 cooking pots and other domestic containers from Palermo and rural Casale San Pietro. Their sample spans the ninth through twelfth centuries, crossing the Norman conquest. Fats absorbed into pottery can survive long after a meal, making a broken cooking pot an unexpectedly useful record of household work.

The residue study identified animal fats and evidence of plant products, including fruit or grape material. Some pots contained mixed traces. Those combinations could reflect one dish or several meals cooked in the same vessel, so the evidence does not supply a complete medieval recipe.

Clear dairy signals appeared in certain rural cooking wares but not in the sampled Palermo pots. This difference may reflect preparation and supply practices. It does not prove that townspeople never ate cheese: food can reach a table without leaving a trace in its household cooking pot.

The tested pots lacked convincing fish-fat markers. That does not remove fish from the menu: roasting, drying or other preparation can leave different evidence. Archaeology sometimes tells us more about how an ingredient was processed than whether anybody enjoyed eating it.

Sicilian transport jars found on the island, in Sardinia and at Pisa contained chemical evidence consistent with grape products. Researchers interpret the ninth to eleventh-century vessels as evidence of a substantial wine trade across the Mediterranean. Food containers can reveal journeys that written histories barely mention.

A wine cargo does not identify the religion of the person who bought or drank it. The evidence shows production and exchange within an island ruled by Muslims, not that every merchant or household followed the same drinking habits.

A detailed study of Palermo’s late ninth to eleventh-century pottery compares shapes, fabrics and production methods. These ordinary containers help researchers date settlement layers and reconstruct workshop activity. A plain vessel can be more useful for sorting archaeological chronology than an impressive object without a known context.

The same ceramic research investigates where Palermo’s products circulated. Comparing locally made vessels with finds elsewhere helps distinguish production from distribution. It is evidence for economic connections, rather than a reason to imagine every surviving pot was made in the capital.

Around Castronovo, the Sicily in Transition project studies fortifications alongside the long-lived rural settlement of Casale San Pietro. The sites changed across Byzantine, Islamic and Norman periods. Looking beyond palaces reveals how roads, farms and settlements connected the island’s countryside to changing centers of power.

A gold quarter-dinar minted in Sicily in 1029 survives in the British Museum. It measures only 14 millimeters across and weighs 0.96 grams. Its Arabic legends name authority through writing rather than a ruler’s portrait: a tiny object carried a political message as well as monetary value.

The Arabic poet Ibn Hamdis was a Sicilian who made a literary career abroad after leaving his homeland. His later poetry is an important voice of displacement and memory. It should be read as one person’s crafted experience, not as a census of everyone who stayed or departed.

In a later exile poem, Ibn Hamdis writes “فإن كنتُ أخرجت من جنةٍ” ,  “If I have been driven out of a paradise.” The Arabic survives in his transmitted poetry. This is a retrospective literary image of his lost homeland, not an inscription dated to Kalbid rule.

ending.text: Norman conquest ended independent Muslim governments on the island by 1091. The fall of governments did not instantly erase Muslim communities, Arabic writing or established farming and craft traditions. The map label’s 1100 endpoint rounds past the political conquest.
